seoTitle: Free Hex Dump Viewer: hexdump -C Style Output
metaDescription: See text or pasted hex bytes as a classic hexdump -C view with offsets, hex columns and an ASCII panel. Free, runs in your browser.
intro: Paste text or hex bytes and get a hexdump -C style listing with the offset, bytes in hexadecimal and a printable ASCII column for each row.
why:
When a file or a string misbehaves, looking at the real bytes often settles it: a byte order mark at the start, a carriage return before a line feed, a non-breaking space that looks like a normal one, or a character that took three bytes instead of one. A hex dump makes these differences visible.

This viewer encodes your text as UTF-8 and prints rows of 16 bytes by default, split into two groups of eight, with a final offset giving the total length. You can also paste hex bytes from a log or a packet capture to get the same layout. It does not read files from disk, so for a file, copy its bytes as hex first.
howTo: Paste text, or choose hex and paste byte values.
Set the number of bytes per row, between 4 and 64.
Read the offsets, hex columns and ASCII panel in the output.

faq.q: How is text turned into bytes?
faq.a: As UTF-8. Plain ASCII uses one byte per character, accented letters use two, and the euro sign uses three, so the dump shows the true size of your string.

faq.q: What input formats work for hex?
faq.a: Pairs of hex digits, optionally with spaces, colons, commas, 0x prefixes or a leading 0x. The number of digits must be even or the tool reports an error.

faq.q: What do the dots in the ASCII panel mean?
faq.a: Bytes that are not printable ASCII, such as control characters and parts of multibyte letters, are shown as a dot, exactly as hexdump does.

faq.q: Can I open a file directly?
faq.a: No. This tool takes text or hex pasted into the box. It is meant for small samples, not large binary files.
